title: What is the difference between a unique index and a clustered index?
shortTitle: What is the difference between a unique index and a clustered index

s1_definition.profdef: A unique index is a logical constraint plus a lookup structure that guarantees no two rows share the same value in the indexed columns; its purpose is correctness and fast equality lookup, and a table can have many unique indexes. A clustered index is a physical storage decision: it defines the order in which the table's rows are actually stored on disk, so the leaf level of the clustered index is the table itself, and a table can have at most one. The two are independent concepts — an index can be unique but not clustered, clustered but not unique, both, or neither.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a unique index is a rule written on a form: "no two accounts may have the same PAN number." The clerk checks the rule and rejects duplicates, and the bank can enforce many such rules at once (unique PAN, unique email, unique Aadhaar). A clustered index is how the physical account folders are arranged in the vault: the folders are stored in account-number order, one single arrangement, because a folder can physically sit in only one place. You can have many rulebooks (unique indexes) but only one physical ordering of the folders (clustered index).
s1_definition.oneliner: Unique is a correctness rule about values you can have many of; clustered is the single physical order of the rows you can have only one of.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A unique index is a logical constraint plus a lookup structure that guarantees no two rows share the same value in the indexed columns; its purpose is correctness and fast equality lookup, and a table can have many unique indexes. A clustered index is a physical storage decision: it defines the order in which the table's rows are actually stored on disk, so the leaf level of the clustered index is the table itself, and a table can have at most one. The two are independent concepts — an index can be unique but not clustered, clustered but not unique, both, or neither.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a unique index is a rule written on a form: "no two accounts may have the same PAN number." The clerk checks the rule and rejects duplicates, and the bank can enforce many such rules at once (unique PAN, unique email, unique Aadhaar). A clustered index is how the physical account folders are arranged in the vault: the folders are stored in account-number order, one single arrangement, because a folder can physically sit in only one place. You can have many rulebooks (unique indexes) but only one physical ordering of the folders (clustered index).

**One line to remember:** Unique is a correctness rule about values you can have many of; clustered is the single physical order of the rows you can have only one of.

sections.s2_technical:
A unique index serves two jobs. First, it enforces a business rule: the engine rejects any insert or update that would create a duplicate in the indexed columns, so it protects data integrity at the database layer where it cannot be bypassed by application bugs. Second, because the values are unique and indexed, equality lookups are extremely fast and the planner knows at most one row can match. You can declare several unique indexes on one table — for example unique PAN, unique email, and unique mobile number all at once.

A clustered index is about physical layout, not uniqueness. It dictates that the table rows are stored sorted by the clustered key, so the clustered index's leaf pages are the data pages themselves. Because rows can only be physically ordered one way, there is exactly one clustered index per table. Reaching a clustered key gives you the whole row immediately with no secondary lookup, which makes range scans on the clustered key very fast.

The concepts combine freely. In SQL Server and InnoDB the primary key is by default both unique and clustered. But you can have a clustered index that is not unique (for example clustering a huge log table by date, which has duplicates), and you can have many unique indexes that are all non-clustered (unique PAN and unique email are both separate non-clustered structures pointing back to the clustered rows).

A senior nuance worth stating: in InnoDB every non-clustered (secondary) index leaf stores the clustered key as its row pointer, so a wide clustered key bloats every secondary index and every secondary lookup does two traversals — first the secondary index to get the clustered key, then the clustered index to get the row. This is why banks pick a compact clustered key. Another nuance: PostgreSQL does not keep a table permanently clustered; its `CLUSTER` command reorders once and the order drifts as rows change, so PostgreSQL's "primary key" is really a unique non-clustered index over a heap, unlike SQL Server or InnoDB.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Compliance must guarantee that no two customers can be registered with the same PAN and no two with the same email, even if two requests race. This is exactly a unique index: the database rejects the duplicate regardless of application logic, and we need two of them.

Problem 2 — The accounts table is queried mostly by account id in ranges and point lookups, and we want reaching the key to hand back the whole row with no extra hop. This is exactly a clustered index on the account id.

Problem 3 — An audit-log table has billions of rows mostly queried by date, with many rows sharing the same timestamp. This is exactly a non-unique clustered index: clustered for fast date ranges, but not unique because duplicates are expected.

The mini-project defines an accounts table with a clustered primary key and two unique indexes, plus an audit table with a non-unique clustered index on date, and a service that inserts a duplicate PAN to show the unique index rejecting it.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/unique-clustered-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# Show the clustered PK range scan returns whole rows with no bookmark lookup
sqlcmd -Q "SET SHOWPLAN_TEXT ON; SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE id BETWEEN 'A' AND 'S';"

# Show the unique index rejecting a duplicate PAN
curl -X POST http://localhost:8080/api/v1/register \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"id":"SAV9999","holderName":"Imposter","pan":"ABCDE1234F","email":"x@bank.in","balance":0}'
# Expect: 409 Conflict — duplicate PAN rejected by ux_accounts_pan
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a registration request for a new account SAV9999 that reuses Rajesh's PAN ABCDE1234F.

Step 1 — The service calls `repo.save(account)`, which issues an INSERT into the accounts table.

Step 2 — The engine first places the row according to the clustered index on id. Because the table is physically ordered by id, SAV9999 is slotted into its correct physical position among the data pages.

Step 3 — Before the insert commits, the engine checks every unique index. The unique index on PAN already contains ABCDE1234F for SAV2001, so the new row violates uniqueness.

Step 4 — The database aborts the insert and raises a constraint violation. The application catches it as a data-integrity exception and translates it into a 409 Conflict with a clear message.

Step 5 — A later valid lookup `findByPan('PQRSX9876L')` uses the unique index to jump straight to Priya's single row, and a range query on id uses the clustered index to read whole rows in order without any secondary hop.

```text
2026-10-25 14:36:06 SEVERE RegistrationService - Duplicate PAN or email rejected by unique index: ux_accounts_pan
2026-10-25 14:36:07 INFO  RegistrationService - Registered account SAV9999 (clustered PK), PAN/email uniqueness enforced
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  INSERT account SAV9999 (PAN=ABCDE1234F, duplicate)
    │
    ▼
  Clustered index (id) → find physical slot for SAV9999
    │
    ▼
  Check UNIQUE ux_accounts_pan
    ├─ PAN ABCDE1234F already exists (SAV2001)
    │     │
    │     ▼
    │   VIOLATION → abort → 409 Conflict
    │
    └─ (if unique) → also check ux_accounts_email → COMMIT

  LOOKUP findByPan('PQRSX9876L')
    │ unique index seek → exactly 1 row (Priya)
    ▼
  RANGE on id → clustered index → whole rows in order, no bookmark lookup
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A unique index and a clustered index solve completely different problems, and I always separate them clearly in an interview. A unique index is a correctness guarantee: it ensures no two rows share the same value in the indexed columns, so the database itself rejects duplicates where no application bug can slip past, and it also makes equality lookups fast because the planner knows at most one row matches. Crucially, a table can have many unique indexes — unique PAN, unique email, unique mobile number all at once.

A clustered index is a physical storage decision: it defines the order in which the rows are actually written to disk, so the leaf level of the clustered index is the table data itself. Because rows can only be physically arranged one way, there is exactly one clustered index per table, and reaching a clustered key hands back the whole row with no secondary lookup, which makes range scans on that key very fast. The two concepts are independent — you can have a clustered index that is not unique, like a log table clustered by date with duplicate timestamps, and many unique indexes that are all non-clustered.

At the National Bank of India I used both deliberately. The accounts table had a clustered primary key on account id for fast id ranges that return full rows directly, plus two separate non-clustered unique indexes on PAN and email so compliance was guaranteed at the database level even under racing requests. Our audit log, by contrast, had a clustered but non-unique index on event date, because we query it by date range and many events share the same timestamp.

The nuance I like to add is that in InnoDB every secondary index stores the clustered key as its row pointer, so a wide clustered key silently bloats every other index and doubles the traversals on a secondary lookup. That is exactly why we keep the clustered key compact. And I note that PostgreSQL differs: its primary key is really a unique non-clustered index over a heap, and its CLUSTER command only reorders once rather than keeping the table permanently clustered.

keyPoints: Index: data structure for fast lookup — B-tree most common
Speeds up WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY — slows down INSERT/UPDATE
Composite index: left-prefix rule — order matters
Covering index: all query columns in index — no table lookup needed
